title: I've played with and against Erling Haaland and this is the only way to stop him, it's different to Harry Kane | talkSPORT
text:
It's a problem dozens of defenders have been forced to deal with and most haven't worked it out yet.

This is evidenced by the fact the Norway international boasts an absurd record of 162 goals from 198 games for Manchester City across all competitions.

Brazil was the latest party burdened by Haaland, as his two goals in 11 minutes secured a shock 2-1 result for Norway in their World Cup round of 16 encounter.

Haaland's first was emblematic of his nose for goal, waiting for the perfect time to out-leap Gabriel and thump a header home.

Gabriel, who has developed a rivalry with Haaland in the Premier League, lay flat on his back following the opener, knowing his long-time adversary got the better of him.

The 25-year-old's second was slightly more unusual as he drilled an effort from outside the box along the turf and past a sprawling Alisson.

In essence, both of Haaland's goals underlined why he gives defenders nightmares.

However, it is possible to stop the man many deem an unstoppable force.

Odin Bjortuft was tasked with defending Haaland when Manchester City travelled to face Norwegian side Bodo/Glimt in the Champions League last January.

On paper, it was very much a David versus Goliath battle.

According to Transfermarkt, Bodo's squad value is nearly £71million while City's is an astronomical £1.22b.

However, it was the underdogs who won 3-1 in front of an 8,016-strong crowd at the Aspmyra Stadion in Bodo, a town located north of the Arctic Circle.

Haaland, who played the entire contest, was locked up superbly by Bjortuft and his fellow centre-back Jostein Gundersen.

The City superstar ended the game with three shots, but all were off target.

Besides playing against him, Bjortuft also spent time playing alongside Haaland when he was called up to Norway's pre-World Cup camp in March.

"I think it's difficult, no doubt," Bjortuft exclusively told talkSPORT.com when asked how to stop Haaland.

"He's world class. He's really good at timing when he turns on. If it's a few minutes during a game, it's a hat-trick.

"As a defender, you always have to be aware of him and watching closely. If you slip for a second, then you're 1-0 down.

"I think it's almost impossible to manage him on your own. You have to work as a team and as centre backs, you have to work together, maybe 2 against 1 against him, because his abilities are insane, really.

"It's difficult, but you have to do it as a team to stop him, not individually."

The win over City was just one moment of a memorable Champions League campaign for Bodo.

They rounded out the league phase with a 2-1 win away at eventual semi-finalists Atletico Madrid before stunning Inter Milan 5-2 on aggregate in the knockout phase play-offs.

Sadly Bodo's Champions League adventure ended in the round of 16 at the hands of Sporting, but the run of results proved the Norwegian side belongs among Europe's elite.

Bjortuft's advice will certainly be welcomed by Ezri Konsa and Marc Guehi, who look likely to be England's centre-back pairing for their World Cup quarter-final clash against Norway on Saturday.

Funnily enough, Konsa, who plays for Aston Villa, has been one of the select few who has successfully managed to keep Haaland quiet.

In the five league fixtures against Villa when Konsa has played, Haaland has scored only once from 406 minutes.

Guehi will also know all of Haaland's tricks given the two have been teammates at City since the former joined from Crystal Palace in January.

Unfortunately for Norway, their defenders will have to try and contain England's very own goalscoring machine in Harry Kane.

After a season with Bayern Munich where he netted a mind-boggling 61 goals in 51 games, Kane has very much picked up where he left off, scoring six times for England at this World Cup.

But trying to defend Kane is an entirely different puzzle compared to stopping Haaland.

Bjortuft is yet to face Kane in his career, but having watched several of his matches for club and country, he has a good idea on what would be needed.

"It's a big difference of course," Bjortuft said.

"Harry is dropping a lot, so you have to leave some of the responsibility to the midfielders sometimes.

"But it's the same [as with Haaland]. When he gets the ball, you have to be really aware of what's going on around you. He's not just a goalscorer, he sets up his wingers one by one all the time against the goalkeeper. When he drops, you have to be aware.

"And if he gets an inch of a space inside the 16-yard box, he will probably score a goal.

"You have to be really close up on him and take him a different way to Haaland. Haaland is really explosive and you have to manage the space a bit more. Harry, you have to be really tight on him so he doesn't get his right foot or left foot open."
